title: Position-table proportional-derivative control
physicalPurpose: Move a payload carriage promptly without excessive overshoot, oscillation, or motor torque.
principalTechnique: Derivative velocity feedback for mechanical damping
objective: Add derivative action to the position controller, then explain from the mechanics why velocity feedback reduces overshoot without changing the proportional stiffness.

simplifications: The table and payload remain one rigid rotational inertia so derivative damping is isolated.
The encoder is noise-free in this lesson; quantization, noise and filtering are introduced in Lesson 23.

baseline.limitation: The stiff proportional controller reaches the target quickly but overshoots and continues oscillating.

change.decision: Keep proportional stiffness fixed and accept derivative action only if it materially reduces overshoot and late position movement without violating the torque limit.

abortPredicates: Position, velocity or torque is nonfinite
Applied torque leaves -10 to 10 N m
simulationOnlyRestrictions: Simulation results do not qualify derivative action on a physical axis or noisy encoder.

video.viewerOutcome: Explain derivative velocity feedback as damping and select PD from measured overshoot, late movement, and torque evidence.

learning.context: The same motor-driven positioning table must retain its proportional stiffness while reducing the oscillation observed in Lesson 19.
learning.reason: Raising or lowering Kp moves speed and stiffness together; a separate velocity-dependent torque is needed to add damping.
theory: Angular velocity (omega) is the measured rate of position change in radians per second. Derivative action uses that motion to oppose movement.

The derivative gain (Kd) states the opposing torque requested per radian per second and uses newton-metre-seconds per radian. With derivative setpoint weight zero, derivative torque T_D equals minus Kd times omega.
The proportional torque T_P equals Kp times error e. The requested motor torque T_requested is T_P plus T_D, and applied motor torque T_applied is the result after the drive clamp.

Phase lead means the derivative path reacts to motion before position error reaches its later peak. The damping ratio (zeta) compares total damping with the critical damping needed to avoid oscillation.

A PD controller cannot supply nonzero equilibrium torque at zero position error and zero velocity; constant friction or load torque therefore creates offset unless bias or integral action supplies it.
learning.workedPrediction: With J 1 kg m2, B 1 N m s/rad and Kp 8 N m/rad, Kd 0 gives damping ratio 0.177 while Kd 3 gives 0.707. At a one-radian initial error proportional torque requests 8 N m; at 1 rad/s positive velocity, Kd 3 requests -3 N m derivative torque, leaving 5 N m combined request before limits.
practicalPreparation: Confirm the same table, one-radian step, 20 ms cycle, zero initial position and velocity, plus or minus 10 N m limit, and zero-torque safe state.
learning.baseline: Run Kp 8 with Kd 0 and record overshoot plus the maximum-minus-minimum position span from 5 to 15 seconds.
learning.change: Restore the same state and repeat with Kp unchanged at 8 and Kd set to 3; derivative remains on measurement through c equal to zero.
learning.comparison: Compare position overshoot, late position span and applied torque on equal axes under identical conditions.
learning.validation: Require PD overshoot at most 0.1 rad and at most one quarter of P overshoot, late span at most one fifth of the P result, finite signals, and applied torque within plus or minus 10 N m.
learning.explanation: Explain why velocity-opposing torque removes mechanical energy without changing the position-error stiffness set by Kp.
learning.transfer: Use PD when added damping is needed and equilibrium actuation is zero or supplied separately; Lesson 21 adds constant load torque and exposes the remaining position offset.
